title: Merge Sort
definition: Merge Sort is a highly efficient, stable comparison sort based on the divide-and-conquer paradigm. It works by recursively dividing the array into two halves until each subarray has one element, then merging the subarrays in a sorted manner until the entire array is sorted.
conceptExplanation: Merge Sort follows divide-and-conquer: 1) Divide the unsorted array into n subarrays, each containing one element (a list of one element is considered sorted). 2) Repeatedly merge subarrays to produce new sorted subarrays until there is only one subarray remaining. This final array is the sorted result. It guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases and is stable (maintains relative order of equal elements).
keyPoints: - Divide and conquer - Recursive division - Merge step - Stable sort - O(n log n) all cases
importantTerminology: Merge Sort, Divide, Merge, Stable sort, Temporary array
workingPrinciple: The algorithm recursively divides the array into two halves until each subarray has a single element. Then, it merges the subarrays by comparing elements from each and placing the smaller element into a new temporary array. The merge process continues up the recursion tree until the entire array is sorted. Key: the merge step is where the actual sorting happens. Uses a temporary array of size n for merging.
realLifeExample: Sorting linked lists, external sorting, stable sort required scenarios
dsaExample: Sorting array [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]: divide → [38,27,43,3] and [9,82,10] → further divide → merge sorted subarrays → [3, 27, 38, 43] and [9, 10, 82] → merge → [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]
diagram: Merge sort divide and merge: [38,27,43,3,9,82,10] → divide to single elements → merge [38,27] → [27,38], merge [43,3] → [3,43], merge [27,38] with [3,43] → [3,27,38,43], merge [9,82] → [82,9] wait correct → [9,82], merge [9,82] with [3,27,38,43] → [3,9,10,27,38,43,82] sorted
algorithm:
Merge Sort Algorithm:
1. MERGESORT(arr, l, r)
2. IF l < r
3.   SET m = floor((l + r) / 2)
4.   MERGESORT(arr, l, m)
5.   MERGESORT(arr, m + 1, r)
6.   MERGE(arr, l, m, r)
7. END IF

MERGE(arr, l, m, r):
1. Create temporary array temp[] of size r-l+1
2. SET i = l, j = m + 1, k = 0
3. WHILE i <= m AND j <= r
4.   IF arr[i] <= arr[j]
5.     SET temp[k] = arr[i]
5.   SET i = i + 1
6.   ELSE
5.     SET temp[k] = arr[j]
5.   SET j = j + 1
6.   END IF
6.   SET k = k + 1
7. END WHILE
7. COPY remaining elements of left half: WHILE i <= m: temp[k] = arr[i]; i++; k++
8. COPY remaining elements of right half: WHILE j <= r: temp[k] = arr[j]; j++; k++
9. COPY temp[] back to arr[l..r]
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  FUNCTION mergesort(arr, l, r)
    IF l < r
      SET m = floor((l + r) / 2)
      mergesort(arr, l, m)
      mergesort(arr, m + 1, r)
      merge(arr, l, m, r)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  FUNCTION merge(arr, l, m, r)
    CREATE temp[l..r]
    SET i = l, j = m + 1, k = 0
    WHILE i <= m AND j <= r
      IF arr[i] <= arr[j]
        SET temp[k] = arr[i]
        SET i = i + 1
      ELSE
        SET temp[k] = arr[j]
        SET j = j + 1
      END IF
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    WHILE i <= m
      SET temp[k] = arr[i]
      SET i = i + 1
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    WHILE j <= r
      SET temp[k] = arr[j]
      SET j = j + 1
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    COPY temp[k] back to arr[l..r]
  END FUNCTION
END
complexity:
Time: Always O(n log n) - best, average, and worst case\nSpace: O(n) - temporary array needed for merging (not in-place)
Stable: Yes (arr[i] <= arr[j] maintains relative order of equal elements)

Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → Master theorem gives O(n log n)
applications: When stable sort is required, linked lists, external sorting, when worst-case O(n log n) is needed
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) time in all cases, stable sort, simple concept, works well for linked lists
limitations: O(n) extra space required, not in-place, recursive overhead, slightly slower than quick sort in practice due to extra memory
commonMistakes: Not using stable comparison (arr[i] < arr[j] vs arr[i] <= arr[j]), incorrect temporary array copying, off-by-one in merge logic, not handling remaining elements after main loop
importantExamPoints:
Always O(n log n) best/average/worst - guaranteed\nStable sort (arr[i] <= arr[j] condition)
O(n) extra space for temporary array
Works well for linked lists (O(1) extra space with pointer changes)
Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) → O(n log n) by master theorem
Not suitable for large arrays where memory is constraint

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain merge sort algorithm and complexity analysis.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It divides the array into two halves recursively until each subarray has one element, then merges the subarrays in sorted order.

Algorithm: MERGESORT(arr, l, r): if l < r, find mid = floor((l+r)/2), recursively sort left and right halves, then MERGE(arr, l, m, r).

Merge step: Creates temporary array, compares elements from left and right halves, places smaller element first, copies remaining elements.

Complexity:
- Time: Always O(n log n) for best, average, and worst case
- Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)
- By master theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=Θ(n), log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1, since f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a))), case 2 applies → T(n) = Θ(n log n)
- Space: O(n) for temporary array used in merge
- Not in-place (requires auxiliary array of size n)
- Comparisons: ~n log n / 2 on average

Key Features:
- Guaranteed O(n log n) performance - no worst case like quick sort
- Stable sort (maintains relative order of equal elements due to arr[i] <= arr[j])
- Works well for linked lists (can merge with O(1) extra space)
- Not in-place - requires temporary array of size n

Applications: Stable sort required, linked lists, external sorting (merge files), worst-case O(n log n) needed.

Comparison: vs Quick Sort: merge sort guaranteed O(n log n), stable, but uses O(n) space vs quick sort's O(log n) space and possible O(n²) worst case. vs Heap Sort: both O(n log n), heap sort in-place O(1) space but not stable.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain merge sort with algorithm, pseudocode, complexity, and applications.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Merge Sort: 

Algorithm: Uses divide-and-conquer. Divide the unsorted list into n sublists, each containing one element (a list of one is considered sorted). Repeatedly merge sublists to produce new sorted sublists until there is only one sublist remaining.

Pseudocode:
BEGIN
  FUNCTION mergesort(arr, l, r)
    IF l < r
      SET m = floor((l + r) / 2)
      mergesort(arr, l, m)
      mergesort(arr, m + 1, r)
      merge(arr, l, m, r)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  FUNCTION merge(arr, l, m, r)
    CREATE temp[l..r]
    SET i = l, j = m + 1, k = 0
    WHILE i <= m AND j <= r
      IF arr[i] <= arr[j]
        SET temp[k] = arr[i]
        SET i = i + 1
      ELSE
        SET temp[k] = arr[j]
        SET j = j + 1
      END IF
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    WHILE i <= m
      SET temp[k] = arr[i]
      SET i = i + 1
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    WHILE j <= r
      SET temp[k] = arr[j]
      SET j = j + 1
      SET k = k + 1
    END WHILE
    COPY temp back to arr[l..r]
  END FUNCTION
END

Complexity Analysis:
- Time: Θ(n log n) for all cases (best, average, worst)
- Recurrence relation: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)
- By master theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=Θ(n), log_b(a)=1, case 2 → T(n)=Θ(n log n)
- Space: Θ(n) for temporary array (not in-place)
- Number of comparisons: between n log n / 2 and n log n depending on data

Key Features:
- Guaranteed O(n log n) - no worst case like quick sort's O(n²)
- Stable sort: arr[i] <= arr[j] condition preserves relative order of equal elements
- Not in-place - requires auxiliary array of size n
- Good for linked lists: can merge with O(1) extra space by pointer manipulation
- Recursion depth: log n

Comparison with Other Sorts:
- vs Quick Sort: Merge sort guaranteed O(n log n), stable, uses O(n) space. Quick sort faster in practice, in-place O(log n) space, not stable, worst O(n²).
- vs Heap Sort: Both O(n log n). Heap sort in-place O(1) space, not stable. Merge sort stable, uses O(n) space.
- vs Insertion Sort: O(n log n) vs O(n²). Insertion sort adaptive, good for small/nearly sorted data.

Applications:
1. When stable sort is required (e.g., sorting by multiple keys)
2. Linked list sorting (O(1) extra space with pointer changes)
3. External sorting / merge sort for large files
4. When worst-case O(n log n) is mandatory
5. Parallel execution (divide phases can run in parallel)

Practical: JavaScript's Array.sort() uses Timsort (merge/insertion hybrid) in modern engines.
